correctness.rationale: The regular language \(1(1\mid00)^*\) partitions adjacent accepted words into first-divergence witnesses indexed by a valid prefix and an integer remaining length. The exact extremal completions are \(p00\,1^{r-1}\) and \(p1\,0^r\) (even \(r\)) or \(p1\,0^{r-1}1\) (odd \(r\)); these prove adjacency and account for every same-length pair. The counts are \(F_{m-r-1}\) by a direct terminal-block recurrence, and crossing length classes adds only gaps 1 and 2. Summation proves the stated finite histogram. Limiting laws follow from Binet ratios, and independent brute-force verification passed for all \(2\le M\le16\). Boundary cases \(M=2,3\) and odd/even parity are included.

originality.rationale: OEIS A060142 enumerates the underlying set and its self-generating recurrences but does not state a complete successive-gap histogram, all-scale Fibonacci multiplicities or limiting heavy-tailed law. Merta 2018 §2 gives the same set, an exact fixed-bit-length set recursion and a parity/Fibonacci-word coding of accepted positions; it does not give the all-gap histogram. Merta Theorem 4.6 treats successive differences of the 1-support of a formal-power-series inverse, not differences of the Baum–Sweet 1-support, and therefore does not dominate this claim. Kimberling 2000 considers a genuinely different generator \(1,2x,4x-1\). Dreyfus–Hardouin–Roques 2015 concerns transcendence, not local gaps. No implication covering the claimed histogram was identified in actual direct and semantic searches. Historical priority remains subject to inaccessible original full text and the non-exhaustiveness of literature search.

value.rationale: Consecutive distances between 1-symbols are the return-gap spectrum of a classical automatic word with unbounded zero runs. The theorem classifies every possible gap and its exact multiplicity at every dyadic size, yielding a nondegenerate limiting distribution with a power-law tail and infinite mean. This uniform structural law is stronger than providing the underlying support or numerically listing its first differences; it quantifies a natural recurrence/sparsity statistic and its scale dependence.
